claims.claim: She has carried a stage name she tried to drop: Rolling Stone (2021) reports she "has tried a few times over the years to change it and was persuaded otherwise by a former manager," and quotes her: "My image was the pothead hippie girl, and I'm not that."
claims.passage: reported that she "has tried a few times over the years to change it and was persuaded otherwise by a former manager." Her explanation: "My image was the pothead hippie girl, and I'm not that."
claims.inference: A long-running, costly instance of living inside a frame someone else preferred: she objected, was talked out of it, and still uses the name. Supports inertia toward her own agenda. The attempt to change it is the writer's report (presumably from her); only the second sentence is a direct quote. Edit stage: the article no longer counts the name as an "eruption" or as order evidence; it is reported as what the source shows (she objected, was persuaded, kept it).
claims.alternative: A stage name with a hit catalogue attached is a commercial asset; staying with it can be plain business sense, and many artists dislike early names without it meaning anything about temperament. No date or detail of the attempts is given.
claims.review_trigger: If she changes or retires the stage name, or dates the attempts to change it, update "As of 2026 the name is still on the marquee."

claims.claim: To Missy Elliott in 2021: "About 98 percent of the time I'm just trying to have fun. But sometimes there's people in the studio who are like, 'This would be a great TikTok song.' I'm not really trying to fight them and I get it, so I try to be open-minded." When Elliott described doing records "that didn't feel like you," she answered: "I did that three or four times. claims.passage: "About 98 percent of the time I'm just trying to have fun," she said. "But sometimes there's people in the studio who are like, 'This would be a great TikTok song.' I'm not really trying to fight them and I get it, so I try to be open-minded."
claims.inference: Her stated reason for going along is avoiding the fight ("not really trying to fight them"), not doubt about her own taste. This is the cleanest contemporaneous statement of the mechanism.
claims.alternative: The same answer opens with "98 percent of the time I'm just trying to have fun," which is Seven language and must be quoted with it. "Three or four times" answers a frame Elliott supplied. Being open to commercial advice is also ordinary professionalism.

claims.claim: In October 2021 she tweeted and immediately deleted: "I'm done saying yes to motherfuckers cuz I cant even have a week to just chill" and "[I] just keep agreeing to shit I dont wanna do in the future. its my own dumb ass fault." Asked about it, she said "I'm really fine," "I don't want people to feel worried or anything like that," and "It feels dramatic." On Instagram Live on 2021-11-24 she said "I feel pressured to do that shit. I don't fucking want to do that. I want to be home. I want to make music. I want to play video games."
claims.passage: "I'm done saying yes to motherfuckers cuz I cant even have a week to just chill," and "[I] just keep agreeing to shit I dont wanna do in the future. its my own dumb ass fault." She deleted them at once. Asked about them, she backed away: "I don't really need people feeling bad for me and shit 'cause I'm really fine." She would not post like that again, she said: "I don't want people to feel worried or anything like that."
claims.inference: A dated, observable cycle at the height of her success: agreeing, resentment surfacing late, a burst, then minimising it so no one is disturbed. She blames her own agreeing, not the people asking.
claims.alternative: Exhaustion during an overbooked album cycle would make almost anyone say this. The tweets survive only in Rolling Stone's transcription. Deleting them may be reputation management advised by a team rather than self-effacement. Edit stage: "She deleted them at once" paraphrases Rolling Stone's "As soon as they appeared on the internet." The retraction ("I'm really fine") is the same reflex she later called "my condition" (C35), so the article does not credit that step to type (C116).

claims.claim: On 2023-05-09 she tweeted: "planet her and hot pink were cash-grabs and yall fell for it," and "now i can go disappear somewhere and touch grass with my loved ones on an island while yall weep for mediocre pop."
claims.passage: "planet her and hot pink were cash-grabs and yall fell for it," and then: "now i can go disappear somewhere and touch grass with my loved ones on an island while yall weep for mediocre pop."
claims.inference: The resentment arrives as an eruption aimed at the audience, and the fantasy attached to it is disappearing somewhere quiet with her people, not a new adventure. Edit stage: used for what she asks for (C114), not as proof that the pop albums were a yes.
claims.alternative: It came during an album announcement and may be a provocation. She presented Planet Her as her own project in 2021 and returned to that lane in 2025 (C105), so the article does not count the pop years as going along.

claims.claim: In December 2023 she said her team makes her keep songs she has cooled on; asked "Have they been right?" she answered "Yeah, they've been right," named "Paint the Town Red," and said its success "was what I was kind of running from a little bit ... I didn't really want to have that pants up high song."
claims.passage: Had they been right? "Yeah, they've been right." She named "Paint the Town Red," the album's No. 1 single, and said its success "was what I was kind of running from a little bit."
claims.inference: Even on the album she made to stop being palatable, she deferred to the room on the most palatable song and it became her biggest hit of the era. She presents it as strategy ("I can be strategic"). Edit stage: used in the Type 6 section as her own statement of taking the room's word on a commercial call.
claims.alternative: She says keeping it was "a smart move," so this can be read as a sound commercial judgment she agrees with, not self-forgetting. Taking a trusted team's call is also what a Six does.

I think that they're a short-lived way of dealing with either anxiety or, you know, pain." A relay of her 2026-08-31 TikToks (S-BA26; the posts were not opened) has stronger wording about drinking. Neither is printed, for length; nothing is sourced to the relay.

claims.inference: Named testimony from one of her managers in 2021, separating the private person from the persona. One of the two third-party observations the surviving separator leans on (C114).
claims.alternative: A manager humanising a client for a cover story, during the Planet Her cycle. In the same paragraph Asrat says "You'd think she just wants to be a housewife." Her other manager Gordan Dillard told Variety in 2023, "It's a performance everywhere we are ... That's her personality" (not printed).

claims.claim: In March 2026, burnt out before the next tour leg, she said "that's just anxiety in a nutshell" and described it as "thinking about the future, overthinking the future."
claims.passage: "just anxiety in a nutshell," which she glossed as "thinking about the future, overthinking the future."
claims.inference: The future shows up as dread, not as plans she is excited about. Cuts against Type 7. Second-transcribed.
claims.alternative: "Overthinking the future" is anticipatory anxiety, the signature of Type 6. The line separates her from a Seven and points toward a Six.

claims.claim: In Sydney in December 2025 Vogue's writer saw her "visibly seize up" when photographed in a shop. She said: "Will I go up to somebody and be like, 'Stop fucking filming me,' and cuss them out? No, I'm not going to do that. I don't want to do that. I think I would rather do it in a creative way," such as looking "purposefully ugly."
claims.passage: Vogue's reporter watched her notice someone photographing her in a Sydney shop in December 2025 and wrote that she "visibly seizes up." Her own rule: "Will I go up to somebody and be like, 'Stop fucking filming me,' and cuss them out? No, I'm not going to do that."
claims.inference: Observed behaviour plus her own rule about strangers. Edit stage: the article claims only that her rule for strangers is restraint; "In person she goes still" was removed.
claims.alternative: Freezing at a camera is a fear response (Six). Not cursing at strangers is ordinary restraint for a celebrity being filmed. Contrary first-hand observations exist and are not printed: Paper (2019) found her "just as ostentatious and provocative IRL as she is online," and Dillard told Variety, "It's a performance everywhere we are."

claims.claim: In 2023 she said: "I love to go to fucking war with trolls. That's just what I've grown up with ... it's just part of me: that I need to respond," and "If somebody wants to fight me on the internet, I will gladly join in, balls to the wall. It's fun for me. I'm a very messy bitch."
claims.passage: "I love to go to fucking war with trolls," she told [Variety](https://variety.com/2023/music/features/doja-cat-new-era-rapping-fashion-1235506581/) in February 2023. A moment later: "If somebody wants to fight me on the internet," she continued, "I will gladly join in, balls to the wall. It's fun for me."
claims.inference: The strongest evidence against a conflict-avoidant reading. The article must quote it. Note the venue she names is the internet and the origin she names is growing up in chat rooms.
claims.alternative: Taken at face value this is a Seven or Eight enjoying the fight, or a counterphobic Six going at the threat. Two quotations separated by an aside; do not join them. Inside the second, Variety's "she continues" interrupts one sentence.

claims.claim: In September 2025, asked why she needs to answer critics: "you can choose to be like, ah, crazy person, I'm scared, and choose flight over fight. But there's also times where I want to turn what I'm saying into a meaningful discussion. And I just enjoy a good debate. But I also like to troll ... That's like my favorite thing to do."
claims.passage: "you can choose to be like, ah, crazy person, I'm scared, and choose flight over fight," but "I just enjoy a good debate. But I also like to troll." Then: "That's like my favorite thing to do."
claims.inference: Her own two-sided answer: flight is the first option she names, trolling the one she enjoys. Second-transcribed; embed candidate for the counter-case.
claims.alternative: An edited network segment; the answer is cut and followed by narration. "Favorite thing to do" is said laughing.

claims.claim: She described her cycle after a blowup: she will say the hostile thing, "And then I'll go 'I'm fine. Everything's fine.' 'Everything's okay, you guys. It's okay.' Like that's my condition," adding "There's a word for it."
claims.passage: "I'm fine. Everything's fine." Then: "Like that's my condition," she said, and "There's a word for it,"
claims.inference: The eruption followed by reflexive smoothing-over, in her words. Because she explains this swing herself, the article does not credit it to type (C116).
claims.alternative: She attributes the cycle to a "condition" with a name she withheld. Second-transcribed at the edit stage (29:53-31:02): "I'll be like, wow, fuck you. And then I'll go, and then I'll go, I'm fine. Everything's fine. Everything's okay, you guys. It's okay. Like that's my condition. That's sort of how that works. It's, there's a word for it, but ... my next challenge is like opening up about those things and saying what that is." The article reports the remark and does not say what the word was.

claims.claim: She called her own public outburst "performative. It was me being like, look how big I am. Look how strong I am," and in 2026 said: "There are little things I do to make people think I don't care, or that I don't feel anything. I do those things on purpose to feel tough. And I am tough. But I'm not that tough. It is a mask."
claims.passage: "What I was doing when I reacted in the way that I reacted was performative. It was me being like, look how big I am. Look how strong I am." To [Elle UK](https://www.elle.com/uk/life-and-culture/a71279884/doja-cat/) in 2026: "I do those things on purpose to feel tough. And I am tough. But I'm not that tough. It is a mask."
claims.inference: Twice, seven months apart, she says the combative front is a show of size put on when she feels exposed. Undercuts reading the outbursts as an Eight's or Seven's native aggression.
claims.alternative: A defensive display of strength against a felt threat is the textbook counterphobic Six. This quotation supports the alternative at least as well as the thesis.

claims.claim: Paraguay, March 2022: after a storm cancelled her festival date and a fan complained she had posted nothing, she replied "I'm sorry"; told it was too late, she replied "I'm not sorry," then tweeted "Everything is dead to me, music is dead, and i'm a f— fool for ever thinking I was made for this" and set her name to "i quit." About 48 hours later: "I do owe people s—. I owe a lot" and "My suffering comes from myself. Not everybody else." On 2022-03-31 she still said she was leaving after her commitments. She did not quit.
claims.passage: she replied, "I'm sorry." Told "it's too late to apologize," she replied, "I'm not sorry," then tweeted "Everything is dead to me, music is dead," called herself a fool "for ever thinking I was made for this," and changed her display name to "i quit." Two days later, [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/music-news/doja-cat-returns-1235049682/) reported, she was back: "I owe a lot." The repair was not tidy: days later, per [Complex](https://www.complex.com/music/a/brad-callas/doja-cat-the-weeknd-after-hours-tour-quitting-music), she told a radio station that doubted her retirement, "Yes the fuck I am." She did not quit.
claims.inference: The one fan dispute on record that shows every step with dates: an apology, a flip when it is refused, collapse into self-blame, a return. Edit stage: the article now says the repair was not clean (she reaffirmed the retirement to a radio station days later, and on 2022-03-31 still said she would leave after her commitments).
claims.alternative: The old page read this as a Seven moving to One. The content is self-doubt, catastrophe and "the death of my fears" (her apology), which fits a Six in a spiral. The tweets are preserved only through outlets; some were deleted. "it's too late to apologize" was a second user's comment; the article gives it in the passive.

claims.claim: Threads, 2023-07-20 to 23: she wrote that fans calling themselves "kittenz" should "get off your phone and get a job and help your parents with the house," and, asked to say she loved them, "I don't though cuz I don't even know ya'll." She deactivated Threads. On 2023-08-16 she posted that the unfollows felt like having "defeated a large beast that's been holding me down" and "I feel free." In December 2023 she said "you'll never see direct quote of me saying I hate my fans."
claims.passage: Fans were demanding a statement about her relationship, [W Magazine](https://www.wmagazine.com/culture/doja-cat-j-cyrus-threads-fans-drama-explained) reported. She refused, wrote that fans who call themselves "kittenz" should "get off your phone and get a job and help your parents with the house," and deactivated the account. On August 16, after unfollows that outlets put at 180,000 to about 500,000, she [posted](https://www.etonline.com/doja-cat-responds-to-fans-who-unfollowed-her-ive-defeated-a-large-beast-209848), "I feel free."
claims.inference: Presented as a dispute that opens with a flat refusal: no accommodation comes first and no repair follows. The trigger is given in the source's own framing (fans demanding a statement about her relationship) with no detail of the third-party allegations.
claims.alternative: Follower losses were reported as more than 180,000 (ET) and about 500,000 (The Fader, Vogue). "I feel free" came about three and a half weeks later in an Instagram Story. The freedom reading of this episode is the Type 7 case and the article now states it (C109). W Magazine quotes her refusal as "I don't give a fuck what you think about my personal life"; that line and "I don't though cuz I don't even know ya'll" were cut for length.

claims.claim: After the first Tour Ma Vie show (Auckland, 2025-11-18) she answered fans on X in separate posts: "I won't and I don't need you"; "I'm not a broadway act"; and "I'm not your fucking costume monkey, I move at my own pace and break my fucking back out there every night ... You are not the artist you are the watcher." She then deleted X from her phone. Later she said she had been "panicking ... really, really on edge" and asking "who's perceiving me?", and: "When I feel that I'm threatened, even though it may not be a threat at all, it rhymes with: You are failing."
claims.passage: [Complex](https://www.complex.com/music/a/alex-ocho/doja-cat-responds-to-fans-criticizing-her-new-tour) collected the replies: "I won't and I don't need you," then a post reading "I'm not your fucking costume monkey, I move at my own pace and break my fucking back out there every night." She told Vogue she then deleted X from her phone; she was back within months.
claims.inference: A dispute that opens with her refusal ("I won't and I don't need you" is the first reply Complex quotes). "I move at my own pace" is a rare first-person statement of tempo.
claims.alternative: Her later explanation is fear of failing under observation (C88): Six, or Three. The "costume monkey" post continues "so you can keep your bullshit opinion to yourself. You are not the artist you are the watcher"; the article stops the quotation at "every night." "Back within months" rests on S-RT26 (published 2026-03-23, second-transcribed at 20:50-21:30): "So yeah, I deleted it. But then I've been on Twitter in the last".
claims.review_trigger: Recheck at each refresh whether she is active on X and reword "she was back within months" if her account says otherwise.

claims.claim: In May 2020 videos surfaced of her in a Tinychat room rumored to be associated with white supremacists, along with a 2015 song titled with a racist slur. Rolling Stone (2021) states there is no evidence the other members were white supremacists and reports her response: a written statement and an Instagram Live in which she denied being "involved in any racist conversations" and said the song was her attempt to reclaim the term.
claims.passage: In May 2020 video surfaced of her in a Tinychat room rumored to be associated with white supremacists, along with a 2015 song titled after a racist slur. Rolling Stone later wrote that there is no evidence the room's other members were white supremacists. She posted a written apology and apologized again on Instagram Live. Per Rolling Stone, she denied being 'involved in any racist conversations' and said the song was her attempt to reclaim a term that had been thrown at her in chat rooms.
claims.inference: FAQ answer. Each allegation it names is paired with her on-record response from an opened print source (S-RS21): the chat room with her denial and Rolling Stone's "no evidence" sentence, the song with her account of it. The apologies rest on S-RS21 ("PR-approved statement") and her own words on the Live ("the apology that i posted," "i'm so sorry if i hurt you guys," S-IGLIVE20).
claims.alternative: Sensitive and contested. Rolling Stone: "There is no evidence the other members of the chatroom were, in fact, white supremacists"; she "denied being 'involved in any racist conversations' on Tinychat" and "says 'Dindu Nuffin' was her attempt to reclaim the term after having it thrown at her by white people in chatrooms." The Live is a fan re-upload read in captions; the edit dropped the captions-only quotation "completely incorrect" in favour of the print wording. The body mentions the episode in one neutral sentence (C112) and sends the reader to this answer.

claims.claim: She signed as a teenager to Dr. Luke's Kemosabe imprint. Asked in 2021 whether she would work with him again she said "That's not a question I feel really comfortable answering," then "There's shit that he's credited for, where I'm like ... 'I don't know if you did anything on that'" and "I don't think I need to work with him again"; weeks later she emailed that she had "no firsthand knowledge" and "The credits on my music are accurate." Vogue reported in March 2026 that she has not worked with him since 2021 and that her association with the imprint is still active.
claims.passage: Dr. Luke is the producer whose Kemosabe imprint signed her as a teenager. Vogue reported in March 2026 that she had not worked with Dr. Luke since 2021, while her association with his Kemosabe imprint was still active. Her 2025 album Vie was released through Kemosabe and RCA. In 2021 she told Rolling Stone, 'I don't think I need to work with him again.' She later emailed the magazine about a different remark from that interview, on songwriting credits, writing, 'The credits on my music are accurate.'
claims.inference: FAQ answer. The follow-up email is now scoped correctly: it clarified a separate remark about songwriting credits ("I may have said something that someone could interpret as me saying that he had taken credit on things he didn't deserve to"), and nothing implies she withdrew "I don't think I need to work with him again." The durable fact is that she stayed on the label and stopped collaborating.
claims.alternative: Sensitive: Kesha's allegations against Dr. Luke involve third parties and are not about Doja Cat; the article does not mention them. Correction to the draft-stage note: an opened source does state his denial. S-RS21 (December 2021): "Dr. Luke has denied Kesha's allegations and sued her for defamation. Kesha dropped her lawsuit in 2016; Dr. Luke's lawsuit is ongoing." That status is as of 2021 and was not rechecked, so an editor who adds the lawsuit must source its current status first. Staying on the label may be contractual, not chosen; the body says so (C113).
claims.review_trigger: Recheck label status and any new collaboration or statement about Dr. Luke before each refresh; the "since 2021" line is Vogue's as of March 2026.

claims.claim: In the first week of August 2022 she shaved her head and eyebrows on Instagram Live and told worried fans "I'm rich, I'm fine." In 2023 she explained: "I wasn't working out and wasn't really taking care of myself in the way that I wanted to. I was like, 'I need to do something,' so I just chopped it all off."
claims.passage: In 2023 she explained to Variety: 'I wasn't working out and wasn't really taking care of myself in the way that I wanted to. I was like, "I need to do something," so I just chopped it all off.'
claims.inference: FAQ only. The shaved-head example was removed from the Type 7 argument because her explanation reads as impulse as easily as anything else.
claims.alternative: The old page read it as a Seven burning down an image. She also said "I needed to change something," which fits that reading. "I'm rich, I'm fine" rests on Stereogum's headline for the 2022-08-05 Live. The FAQ answer also carries "I'm rich, I'm fine" (see C95).

claims.claim: Her two best-known fan disputes (Threads, July 2023; Auckland, November 2025) open with her refusal and end with her leaving the platform.
claims.passage: Where a crowd demanded what she had never given, she refused at once and left the platform.
claims.inference: Scoped to the two bulleted episodes. The draft's running tally ("Leaving the room is her most common ending") and the March 2024 Instagram exit were removed.
claims.alternative: Logging off is standard advice for any celebrity. She returned to X within months (C40); whether she returned to Threads is not established in an opened source, so the article does not say she did.
claims.review_trigger: Recount at each refresh how her dated disputes ended (retraction, exit, return) and keep this sentence scoped to the episodes the page lists.

claims.claim: In August 2025 she said therapy lets her "recognize those things before they happen," see herself as two people, "one of them is a person I'm trying to protect," and that this "has made me feel a lot safer, and I'm big on feeling safe."
claims.passage: therapy taught her to "recognize those things before they happen," and that this "just has made me feel a lot safer, and I'm big on feeling safe."
claims.inference: Her plainest statement of what she values: safety. The central exhibit for Type 6 and it belongs beside the main argument. Second-transcribed; embed candidate.
claims.alternative: The thesis reading is that fear is what breaks through when keeping things smooth fails. That reading cannot be proven from this quote; it has to be argued from what she does when not under threat.

claims.claim: Fear in her own words across five years: "i have a lot of fear in me" (tweet, January 2021); "I'm kind of a snowflake, I'm very sensitive," agreeing people "will ... and they have" used her vulnerabilities against her (2023); "I thought that if I stepped out of my house, something would happen to me, all irrational fear" (2025); "If I have a boyfriend and he leaves just to run errands, my brain thinks he's breaking up with me ... I'm safe" (2026); therapy let her be "at peace without being like, 'I need tarot cards. I need an answer. Text me'" (2026); "The dark side of it is, don't trust everybody" (2021).
claims.passage: in January 2021 she tweeted, per [Complex](https://www.complex.com/music/2021/01/doja-cat-says-shes-not-comfortable-posting-on-tiktok-gaslighting-comments), "i have a lot of fear in me."
claims.inference: The fear vocabulary is not only therapy-era: the 2021 tweet and the 2021 trust line predate it. Anticipating harm, needing reassurance and guarding against betrayal are Six themes.
claims.alternative: Most instances attach to specific exposures (online ridicule, a viral clip, a partner leaving) rather than a standing watchfulness, and she links the attachment fear to her father. She also names a clinical frame for herself (C77). None of this settles motive.

claims.claim: She says she asks to be corrected: of her team, "I have to check them to check me ... I need you to tell me that I'm doing this."
claims.passage: She asks her team to correct her: "I have to check them to check me."
claims.inference: Testing sincerity and recruiting trusted people as a check on herself are characteristic of a Six. Strong evidence for the alternative.
claims.alternative: Second-transcribed at the edit stage (14:36-15:16): "I have to check them to check me, so I'll have to be like, I need this from you. I need you to tell me that I'm doing this, because I'm embarrassed by this thing that I did." Wanting honest feedback is also what years of therapy and public blowups would teach anyone. The flattery line ("it makes me scared," 15:36-16:24, also second-transcribed) was cut for length.

claims.claim: Asked whether she wants to correct misconceptions about her, she said she thinks about them "almost every day" but "It's not for me to prove to people who cannot or don't wish to listen ... instead of ruminating, I can choose to express maybe the way I feel about that thing with music, or with an outfit." In 2023: "I don't need to explain myself ... I don't need to prove myself."
claims.passage: asked whether she wants to correct misconceptions about her, she said, "I think about it almost every day," which is not what self-forgetting sounds like.
claims.inference: The same refusal to argue her case appears in 2021 ("trying to prove myself," C31), 2023 and 2025: she stews, declines the direct fight, and routes it into work. That is steadier than her outbursts and closer to her baseline.
claims.alternative: Daily rumination is not a Nine's forgetting; it reads as Six or Four. And she does answer critics, often (C33, C40). Second-transcribed at the edit stage (36:16-37:08).

claims.claim: In March 2026 she said: "It's incredibly lonely. I'm lonely. I want people to embrace me ... it's also just hard making friends. I don't want to have friends in the industry, so I don't." SZA says: "She's actually a very solitary star ... I think by choice, she shields certain aspects of herself."
claims.passage: "It's incredibly lonely. I'm lonely. I want people to embrace me." [SZA](/personality-analysis/sza), a friend and collaborator, told Vogue: "She's actually a very solitary star."
claims.inference: Complicates the hermit evidence: the withdrawal is not simply contentment. Edit stage: the line was second-transcribed (31:30-33:20) and its referent recorded. She is describing the barrier between herself and people she employs, living far from everyone, and the difficulty of making friends ("I don't want to have friends in the industry, so I don't"); the framing sentence now says that.
claims.alternative: The passage is interrupted by a pet just before the quoted words; the whisper transcription reads "So it's incredibly lonely. I'm lonely. I want people to embrace me." Fame isolates; this may be circumstance. Vogue calls SZA one of her "friends and frequent collaborators."

claims.claim: Evidence for restlessness: "I get bored very easily" and "It might be due to my ADHD" (2023, on switching voices mid-song); "that's my personality is ... I don't like to do the same thing over and over again" (2019); "I didn't have the patience to try and make every song sound similar" (2021); "I love to change my tune and my vibe a lot" and "It's after I make the music that I'm like, 'All right, I'm moving on'" (2025).
claims.passage: "I get bored very easily," she told Variety in 2023, about switching voices inside a song.
claims.inference: The old Type 7 thesis rests on these and readers arriving from "Doja Cat type 7" need to see them. Every one is about musical variety or one over-played song.
claims.alternative: A Seven reading extends them to her whole life. Against that: she says the opposite about rest (C19-C22), stays for years in arrangements she resents (C01, C06), and by 2025 says "I want to do what I know." She attributes the boredom to ADHD herself; no formal diagnosis was found, and it should not be asserted. Edit stage: the ADHD sentence was cut; the article no longer prints a self-attributed condition it cannot check.

claims.claim: Each album has been presented as the real one and then set aside: in 2021 Planet Her was where she would "introduce things ... as opposed to just re-create and rehash"; in May 2023 it and Hot Pink were "cash-grabs"; in September 2025 Scarlet "didn't get me all the way there. So, I want to return back to what I know"; in 2026, "Vie is a reminder that I can go back, or I can do what I want."
claims.passage: Even her 2025 album she described to Elle UK as partly a return: "Vie is a reminder that I can go back, or I can do what I want without having to remain in the state of Scarlet."
claims.inference: The Elle UK sentence is now quoted in full. Its first half is a return to the familiar; its second half ("or I can do what I want") is about not staying put, and the article assigns that half to the Type 7 reading.
claims.alternative: This is the central fact of the Seven reading and an interpretation either way. The serial setting-aside of each era is stated separately (C105).
claims.review_trigger: On her next album or era statement, or any new verdict on Vie, recheck "her 2025 album" and whether she still describes it as a return.

claims.claim: The producer who found her says: "she was a shut-in ... The studio was a safe place for her" and "My first impression of her? I thought she was really shy."
claims.passage: Yeti Beats, the producer who found her music online, told Rolling Stone, "I don't know if she would want me saying this, but she was a shut-in," and, "The studio was a safe place for her."
claims.inference: Independent, named testimony about her at 17-18, before any public persona.
claims.alternative: A teenager in a difficult home; not necessarily the adult. "Safe place" is fear wording and supports the Type 6 reading of those years as much as withdrawal. His hedge is now printed.

claims.claim: Her engineer of roughly seven years says: "she just comes in, and she's so relaxed ... you'll hear her start giggling to herself," calls her "such a lovable weirdo. She's really kind," and says "She never rolls with some big crew of people."
claims.passage: Lewis, of her in the studio, "she just comes in, and she's so relaxed."
claims.inference: First-hand observation of her resting state in the room where she is most at home: easy, amused, low-key, a small circle. Hard to square with a vigilant or driven baseline.
claims.alternative: An employee speaking in a promotional interview. The studio is her comfort zone; it says little about her elsewhere. The article now says most of the calm was described mid-album or mid-tour, by her or by people who work for her.

claims.claim: Her engineer describes her as certain and exacting about the work: she asked to mute Pharrell's verse on "Woman" and wrote her own.
claims.passage: her engineer Rian Lewis told [Revolt](https://www.revolt.tv/article/2023-10-05/328924/how-rian-lewis-realized-doja-cat-is-one-of-the-ballsiest-artists) in 2023 that she once asked to mute a Pharrell Williams verse and try her own. That is an employee describing craft.
claims.inference: Edit stage: no longer used to separate Nine from Six. Certainty about craft, reported by an employee, does not show an absence of doubt where she defers (commercial calls, schedule, people). The article says so and prints her own doubt beside it (C115).
claims.alternative: Lewis's words: "Can we mute his verse? I want to see if I can do something in that space." The Asrat and Marc Jacobs quotations were cut.

claims.claim: Her account of her father, Dumisani Dlamini: in 2019 "I don't hold grudges against him"; in 2026, "my dad left me when I was little."
claims.passage: In an Elle UK interview published that May she said, "my dad left me when I was little."
claims.inference: Her most recent statement on the record, dated by publication (2026-05-14) and placed after his March 2026 denial so the order is true. The article attributes "left" to her and builds nothing on it.
claims.alternative: He disputes it (C64). She was a small child; what she knows of the separation came from her mother (Rolling Stone). Elle UK's writer frames the line as "abandonment issues"; that is the writer's phrase and is not used.
claims.review_trigger: Check for any new statement by her, her father or her mother before each refresh, and at publication.

claims.claim: Her father disputes her account. In April 2020 he told a South African radio host he had been looking for her, that her management blocked him, and "She got hold of me. We spoke. We connected." On 2026-03-23, in videos he later removed, he said "I never left my kid," blamed her mother, and (per Sunday World) said he was turned away from her Pretoria show.
claims.passage: In March 2026, after a TikTok of hers that [Complex](https://www.complex.com/music/a/tracewilliamcowen/doja-cat-father-disputes-deadbeat-label) reported under the label "deadbeat," he said in videos he later removed, "I never left my kid."
claims.inference: His response, dated and placed before her Elle UK statement. What it answered is given in a clause from the Complex reports: her TikTok of 2026-03-20, billed as an entry in "The Deadbeat Chronicles" (S-CXTROLL26); Complex headlined his reply "Father Disputes 'Deadbeat' Label" (S-CXDAD26).
claims.alternative: His videos include accusations against her mother and were taken down; the article quotes only "I never left my kid." The detail of her TikTok is left out. Complex says he "appeared to respond to" her recent claim of difficulty connecting with him while her tour was in South Africa. Her mother has not been heard.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck South African and US coverage for developments (reconciliation, further statements, legal action) before each refresh, and at publication.

claims.claim: She dropped out of high school at 16: "It felt like I was stuck in one spot and everybody else was progressing constantly"; "I definitely didn't like to leave my room. I don't know if I was agoraphobic, but I definitely thought that I was" (2021); "I was agoraphobic, fully" and "I couldn't leave my house" (2026); "I'm in my room all the time, not doing anything. I don't have that many friends" (2021); of learning to sing, "I was so shy ... singing in my room, locking the door."
claims.passage: She dropped out of high school at 16. "I definitely didn't like to leave my room," she told Rolling Stone in 2021. "I don't know if I was agoraphobic, but I definitely thought that I was at the time."
claims.inference: A withdrawn, stalled adolescence in her own words, told the same way in 2019, 2021 and 2026 except that the agoraphobia hardens from "thought that I was" to "fully."
claims.alternative: "Agoraphobic" is her lay description, not a diagnosis; quote it as hers. Fear of leaving the house supports Type 6. She also recalls a period when "all I did was go outside to get the fuck out of the house."

claims.claim: She says "I had a very tough childhood ... growing up like with a single mother is a hard thing to do," that her mother raised five children with "no help" beyond "a lot of aunties," and, asked whether her mother corrects her, "you can see that I never really got checked." Her mother recalls her teenage years: "She was in the room, door closed, constantly creating."

claims.claim: The article's type answer: the record leans Type 9, narrowly and at medium confidence, on the observation that she agrees to things she does not want, objects late, and asks for rest when she objects; Type 6 is a live rival because her own motive words are "safe" and "threatened."
claims.passage: Doja Cat's record leans Enneagram Type 9, the Peacemaker, but narrowly: medium confidence, with Type 6 a live rival. She agrees to things she does not want, objects late, and when she objects she asks for rest and home. Type 6 stays close because her own words for her motive are "safe" and "threatened."
claims.inference: Summary of type_hypothesis in reader language. The stage name and the two albums are no longer listed as things she "erupts" over; the confidence wording matches the one separator that survived review (C114).
claims.alternative: A reader weighting her 2025-26 first-person testimony most heavily can land on Type 6; the article says so in its own section.
claims.review_trigger: At each refresh apply the test in C118: in any newly dated objection, does she name a danger or ask for rest, and off-cycle does she prepare and seek reassurance or do nothing. If new first-hand evidence favours Six, rerun with --refresh --expanded-review.

claims.claim: The order of her yes and her objection does not separate Type 9 from Type 6: a Six can agree to stay safe with people she depends on and turn on them later.
claims.passage: Going along first and objecting late does not separate the two types.
claims.inference: Concession made at the edit stage. The draft offered order as the first discriminator; reviewers showed that an objection always postdates an arrangement, that accommodate-then-erupt is a described Six pattern, and that her stated trigger in June 2025 was a new fact (the clip going viral).
claims.alternative: None; this is the concession itself.
claims.review_trigger: See C90.

claims.claim: The reason for her yes does not separate the two types either: in October 2021 she knew what she did not want and agreed anyway, which is not borrowed certainty, but avoiding a fight is also a way of staying safe.
claims.passage: Nor does the reason for her yes. In October 2021 she knew what she did not want and agreed anyway, which is not borrowed certainty, but avoiding a fight is also a way of staying safe.
claims.inference: The reason test rebuilt on the domain where she defers (obligations she did not want), not on studio precision. It rules out one version of the Six reading (deferring because she doubts her own call) and concedes the other (saying yes because no feels unsafe), which her 2026 words support (C15).
claims.alternative: Her one reason given on the spot, "I'm not really trying to fight them and I get it" (2021), concerns a small studio request she found reasonable.
claims.review_trigger: See C90.

claims.claim: Why the earlier Type 7 read loses: her retreat is to stillness, the future is something she overthinks, and she stayed for years in arrangements she objected to.
claims.passage: It loses on what she does with the claim. As this site reads the type, a Seven reframes an obligation or leaves it. By her own account she keeps meeting it and objects afterward: "[I] just keep agreeing to shit I dont wanna do." And her escape runs home, to a heating blanket, not forward into the next plan
claims.inference: Why the earlier Type 7 read loses, restated against its strongest version (freedom from obligation, C109). "A Seven reframes an obligation or leaves it" is marked as this site's reading of the type, not a sourced fact.
claims.alternative: A Seven reading treats the homebody material as recovery between bursts of stimulation; the second half of her Elle UK sentence about Vie ("or I can do what I want") is left with the Seven (C56). "Keeps meeting it" rests on the October 2021 tweets, which are contemporaneous; the article no longer claims she stayed "for years" in a lane she objected to.

claims.claim: Where Type 6 wins: it takes her stated motive at face value and explains the pre-tour dread, the wish to be checked and the combative display.
claims.passage: The Six reading takes her at her word, and that is its strength: her terms for her own motive are "safe" and "threatened," not peace or ease. It explains the dread before a tour and the wish to be checked, and it reads the online combat as a frightened person making herself large. Weigh her 2025 and 2026 first-person testimony most heavily and you land on Six.
claims.inference: States the alternative at full strength beside the main argument, as the research guardrails require. Rests on C15, C28, C37, C48, C49, C50 and C88.
claims.alternative: The article then argues the Nine stays narrowly ahead on one observation (C114); that step is a judgment, not a proof.

In 2026 she spoke warmly of Planet Her to Elle UK ("taught me I am a lyricist"). Disowning the last era to sell the next is ordinary album-cycle behaviour.

Of the bedroom years before it she said: "I saw potential in myself even though I was still aware it wasn't good. And I really wanted it."

The record shows self-started drive: Billboard has her announcing the song and writing, producing, recording and filming it by the end of the day; Vogue calls it "self-released." No claim of passivity remains on the page.

Her own word for the virality was that it "was definitely not supposed to happen" (S-R1DC19, no longer quoted).

Resisting a claim on her time or pace also fits a Nine or an Eight.

type_hypothesis.against: Her own explanations run on fear and safety, not peace: "I'm big on feeling safe" (2025), "the way I've learned to be safe is to not be honest and not be forthcoming" (2026), "When I feel that I'm threatened ... it rhymes with: You are failing" (2026), "i have a lot of fear in me" (2021), "all irrational fear" (2025, of the opening episode); she asks her team to check her (C15, C48-C50, C88, C110). She says she enjoys the fight: "I love to go to fucking war with trolls ... It's fun for me" (2023), trolling is "my favorite thing to do" (2025), and before fame she spent hours "yelling at and roasting people" (C33, C34, C121). Several of her best-known blowups have no yes in front of them: Threads 2023 and Auckland 2025 open with her refusal, and the March 2026 episode answered no demand at all and was, in her words, a bid for "clicks, likes, approval" (C39, C40, C117, C120). Nearly every blowup answers a claim on her and her payoff word is "I feel free," which is the Type 7 reading at its strongest (C109). She is not short of drive: "Mooo!" was her own project and "I really wanted it" (C108); she presented Planet Her as her own plan and returned to that lane in 2025, so the pop years cannot be counted as going along (C105). She says "I feel most powerful when I am fully in character onstage" and puts a limit on staying home (C111). Her own doubt is on the record ("mid and corny," "fool"), and on a commercial call she took the room's word ("Yeah, they've been right") (C09, C115). She thinks about slights "almost every day" (C52), which is not forgetting. She is lonely, not contentedly withdrawn (C53). The calm of her late teens coincides with heavy cannabis use (C23). Finally, she has her own account of the pattern the thesis started from: the swing from a hostile post to "Everything's fine" is "my condition" (2025), and in March 2026 she said she is "struggling with BPD" and had learned to pretend "to appear like everything is okay" (C35, C77). The article cannot evaluate that account, does not use it as evidence, and does not credit the swing to type (C116). A careful reader could weigh the 2025-26 first-person material most heavily and land on Type 6.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 6 is the strongest rival and explains a great deal. It accounts for the safety and threat vocabulary across 2021-2026; the anticipatory dread ("overthinking the future," C28); the teenage fear of leaving the house and the "safe place" of the studio (C57, C66); the worst-case imagery ("people tearing at my skin," C98) and "all irrational fear" (C110); wanting to be checked (C50); self-doubt (C115); and, as counterphobic defence, the online attacks she herself calls a show of size ("look how big I am," "It is a mask," C37). The edit concedes two things the draft claimed against it. Order does not separate the types: a Six can say yes to stay safe with people she depends on and turn on them later, and "I'm sorry" / "I'm not sorry" fits that ambivalence (C91). The reason for her yes does not separate them either: knowing what she did not want and agreeing anyway is not borrowed certainty, but avoiding a fight is also a way of staying safe, and she says as much in 2026 (C15, C92). Her studio certainty, reported by an employee, is about craft and says nothing about where she defers (C59). Where the Six reading still falls short is narrow: in her dated objections of 2021 and 2023 she asked for rest and home and named no danger or untrustworthy person (C05, C106, C07), and a manager and an engineer described the same resting state (C24, C58); the request for reassurance appears later (C50). Type 7, the published type, explains the boredom line, the humour and the wish to be free of claims on her (C54, C109) but loses on what she does with those claims (she keeps meeting them and objects afterward) and on the direction of her escape, which is home (C20, C93); the second half of her Elle UK sentence about Vie is left with the Seven (C56). Types 3, 4 and 8 each explain a strand and are not disproved (C119).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: After review, one separator is left, and it is narrow. What she asks for: when she objected at the time, before her 2025-26 interviews, she did not name a danger or a person she could not trust. She named rest and home: "a week to just chill" (October 2021, C05), "I want to be home. I want to make music. I want to play video games" (November 2021, C106), "disappear somewhere and touch grass with my loved ones on an island" (May 2023, C07). People around her described the same resting state from outside: "If Amala could stay at home and cook for a month, she would" (Asrat, 2021, C24) and "she just comes in, and she's so relaxed" (Lewis, 2023, C58). The profile's reading, labelled as such in the article, is that a person organized around security, pushed past her limit, asks for reassurance or firmer ground; that request is on her record ("I have to check them to check me," C50) but arrives later, with a therapy vocabulary attached. The draft's two discriminators were withdrawn: order (C91) and reason (C92) are now stated as patterns both types explain, and studio certainty is no longer offered as evidence. Limits, stated plainly on the page: this is a judgment from pattern, not a proof; it treats fear as what breaks through when the smoothing fails rather than as the engine, and the record cannot confirm that (C102). An exhausted Six also wants rest, and fear is on her record in 2021. She has her own account of the blowup-to-"I'm fine" swing, so that swing is not credited to type (C116). Most of the calm was described mid-album or mid-tour, by her or by people who work for her. Confidence is medium and at the low end of medium: the article says "leans Type 9, narrowly," names Type 6 as a live rival, and states what would move the read (C118). If the verifier judges that this separator does not meet the release bar, the correct outcome under the owner note is a hold, not a switch to 6 or a return to 7.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: (1) The pleasure she takes in online combat and in trolling, which she has named as fun since her teens and before fame (C33, C34, C121). (2) The blowups with no yes in front of them, including one she called a bid for approval (C117, C120). (3) Total authority in the studio beside "such an issue with setting boundaries" outside it (C11, C59). (4) Loneliness and wanting "people to embrace me" beside a life arranged for solitude (C53). (5) How far her fear and safety language reflects temperament, therapy, or the condition she says she is struggling with; the article cannot sort these and says so (C72, C77, C116). (6) Whether the stillness of her late teens was temperament or cannabis, and what part drinking played later (C23). (7) Rumination about criticism "almost every day," which fits a Six or Four better than a Nine (C52). (8) The dispute with her father, where the two accounts cannot both be right and neither can be checked (C63, C64). (9) Whether she will actually stop after the tour, and what she does with the quiet if she does (C76). (10) What she gets from the stage, where she says she feels most powerful (C111).
